UOB sells 36 of 38 Marina Collection units within two hours
article:
UOB has sold 36 of the 38 Marina Collection units it put up for sale in under two hours, says Dominic Lee, head of luxury and investment sales at PropNex, the sole marketing agent. Based on listed prices, the units sold for about $103.5 million in total, at an average of $1,342 psf.

Marina Collection is a 124-unit condominium on Cove Drive in Sentosa Cove , next to ONE°15 Marina, and was completed in 2011. It sits on a 99-year lease that started in 2007, with about 79 years remaining.

Bookings opened at 10am on Nov 14, and by 11.40am only two units were left. The two units are still available on a first-come, first-served basis, says Lee.

More than 400 groups viewed the units during previews from Nov 6 to 13. A total of 65 cheques were collected as expressions of interest, which means the sale was 1.7 times subscribed. Balloting was held for 12 units that drew multiple bids.

Of the 36 buyers, 23 were Singaporeans, and seven were Permanent Residents (PRs) from countries ranging from China and India to Guatemala and Turkey. The other six were foreigners: five Americans and one Norwegian, says Lee. Under Singapore’s free trade agreements with the US and Norway, these buyers pay stamp duty at the same rates as Singapore citizens, which means no additional buyer’s stamp duty (ABSD) on a first home, rather than the 60% ABSD most foreigners pay.

Most buyers were owner-occupiers, with 31 units purchased for their own use, he adds. “Buyers loved the marina-facing units, as well as the convenience of being close to three supermarkets." They are Cold Storage and Jasons The Gourmet Grocer at Quayside Isle , and Little Farms at Sentosa Arrival Plaza.

Prices for the units sold ranged from $2.588 million ($1,381 psf) for a 1,873 sq ft three-bedroom unit on the second level, to $3.11 million ($1,301 psf) for a 2,390 sq ft four-bedroom unit with a private enclosed space (PES) on the first level. On a psf basis, prices ranged from $1,269 psf for a first-level four-bedroom unit with PES, to $1,407 psf for a second-level three-bedroom unit.

The two remaining units are both on the first level, include PES, and are tenanted until 3Q2027. One is a 2,099 sq ft three-bedroom unit asking $2.786 million ($1,327 psf). The other is a 2,390 sq ft four-bedroom unit listed at $3.064 million ($1,282 psf).

The sale follows the conclusion of UOB’s long-running lawsuit against the developer, Lippo Marina Collection, which the court found liable for conspiring with buyers to inflate the prices of the same 38 units, sold between 2011 and 2013, through undisclosed “furniture rebates”.

UOB had disbursed about $182 million in housing loans for the units, and all 38 buyers later defaulted. In August, the Appellate Division raised the bank’s damages award from $ 17.7 million to $ 76.1 million, and on Oct 21 corrected it to about $82.4 million to include interest that had been left out.

title: UK's Burnham tries to hush down his own talk of rejoining EU
article:
(Nov 14): Six weeks ago UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested Britain “could go all the way” and rejoin the European Union (EU). This week, he downplayed his own idea: “No one’s talking about rejoining.”

The prime minister heads into a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Nov 20 trying to slow down a conversation he started about the country’s long-term relationship with Europe.

Burnham has been privately making clear to Labour colleagues that he’s not in a rush to decide what he wants his long-term EU policy to be, according to government officials familiar with the matter. Number 10 Downing Street has not even begun discussing which outcome it might favor, according to one. The prime minister is open-minded and keen not to put his thumb on the scale by backing a particular option before much wider consultation with his party, businesses, the public and the EU, they added.

Another official said Burnham’s aides want to tap the brakes on a conversation that’s at risk of getting out of control. In a sign of their caution, Number 10 is undecided on whether to go ahead with a planned speech by Burnham after the summit in which he had intended to set out different options for the future relationship, a third official said. They all spoke on condition of anonymity discussing internal policy deliberations.

Reigniting a debate about Britain’s place in Europe — a decade on from the 2016 referendum — was a decision of Burnham’s own making. In a speech at Labour’s party conference in September and in a round of ensuing media interviews, he said he wanted to begin a discussion about whether the UK should eventually rejoin the bloc, or at least move much closer by entering its single market or a customs union.

Those options all remain on the table but it’ll be some time before Burnham arrives at a preferred route, government officials said. As one put it: it would be wrong to set a direction and then rip the steering wheel off so early in the process when it remains to be seen what voters want and what the EU is prepared to negotiate. An option won’t be chosen in time for the government’s 10 year-plan, set to be laid out by Burnham in December, officials said.

See also: Asda’s flat sales end losing streak as new CEO joins UK grocer

Even though he stressed there would be no major change in Europe policy before the next election, due in 2029, Burnham’s intervention has drawn a mixed reaction from his own Labour Party, as well as from the City of London’s financial sector and other European capitals.

Many in Labour would love to unwind a Brexit decision they see as an historic mistake that’s badly damaged Britain’s global standing and dealt a heavy blow to economic growth. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh are prominent figures backing much closer ties, government officials said.

Yet much of the party sees political risk in returning to free movement of people with the continent and aligning with its rules. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey, Burnham’s de facto deputy Louise Haigh, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper and Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy favour a more cautious approach, the officials said.

See also: Poundland files to delay UK insolvency as it finds a rescuer

All those ministers agree with Burnham that the conversation about Europe should be carefully managed and not pre-determined, views that were expressed at a Cabinet meeting on Tuesday, they said. It is better to have a responsible discussion and get it right, one official said.

However, another characterised the Cabinet divide as all the ministers who have ambitions to be prime minister versus those who want the party to win the next election.

Early feedback from the City of London and businesses has been a factor in tamping down the speculation. While British banks and executives largely backed the campaign to remain in the EU, some industries — particularly financial services and artificial intelligence (AI) — are now reluctant to realign with the bloc’s rules.

Bloomberg reported this week that the UK is opposed to rule-taking on either financial services or AI. A government official said that while they were keeping all options on the table, it would not be Burnham’s preference in any long-term negotiation with the EU to be a rule-taker in these two areas. That implies he would be reluctant to pursue a so-called Norway-style option which amounts to single market membership without being able to influence its rules.

In an intervention earlier this week, David Cameron, the former prime minister who called the 2016 referendum and campaigned unsuccessfully to remain in the EU, told Bloomberg that Britain should not rejoin.

“Instead of launching an argument about rejoining — which I think would be a very long and painful argument and who knows where it would end up — instead of that, focus on how do we be the best friend, best neighbour, best partner,” Cameron said in an interview on The Mishal Husain Show.

For now, Burnham’s priority is finalising a more modest deal at the Friday summit on trade rules for plant and animal products and youth mobility. Before then, on Monday he will deliver a speech on foreign policy in which he’ll repeat his desire for closer relations with Europe.

A government official allied to Burnham said his approach to EU policy would be conversation rather than negotiation, with the aim of fostering a better trade relationship. On the flip side of the argument, another official said it was naive, arguing that Burnham had opened Pandora’s Box without a plan for what he’s trying to achieve.

title: MAS, Bank of England and Bank of Thailand complete FX settlement trial
article:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), Bank of England and Bank of Thailand completed a trial showing how different payment systems could work together to make foreign exchange settlement safer and reduce the cash banks need to settle trades.

More than US$1.4 trillion ($1.8 trillion), or 10% of average daily foreign exchange settlement in April 2025, remained fully exposed to settlement risk, according to Bank for International Settlements. That is the danger that a party to a currency trade pays out money but fails to receive what it is owed.

Project Meridian FX APAC tested payment-versus-payment settlement across the three central banks’ test environments. This ensures that one currency changes hands only if the corresponding payment in the other currency also occurs.

A process known as synchronisation coordinated those payments across separate systems. Partior, a clearing and settlement infrastructure provider, developed, integrated and tested the prototype that linked the transfers.

Alongside individual trades, the project tested whether payments across multiple currency transactions could be offset against one another, reducing the amounts that participants need to pay. Combining that process with linked settlement could help banks use their cash more efficiently while reducing settlement risk.

Testing spanned conventional systems that settle payments individually in real time and systems based on distributed ledger technology. Synchronised settlement worked across systems with different technologies and capabilities, while the trial identified requirements and trade-offs involved in connecting them, the central banks say.

See also: Why the investment industry can’t sit out the anti-scam fight

Earlier Meridian FX work, led by the BIS Innovation Hub in London, provided the foundation for the project. The latest trial extended testing across a broader range of currencies, infrastructures and time zones.

Beyond the technical tests, the project examined legal, regulatory and oversight considerations. The Reserve Bank of Australia and Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas contributed as observers.

Further work could extend the approach to more jurisdictions and industry participants, as well as additional currencies and transaction scenarios. It could also examine the technical, legal, operational and governance arrangements needed to apply synchronised settlement in practice.

See also: How Bpifrance helps French fintechs expand to Southeast Asia

“Cross-border settlement increasingly takes place across systems built on different technologies and operating models. Project Meridian FX APAC has shown how synchronisation could help enable PvP settlement across these diverse environments, reducing settlement risk while supporting greater interoperability,” says Kenneth Gay, chief FinTech officer at the Monetary Authority of Singapore.

Pucktada Treeratpituk, director of Payment Systems and Financial Technology Policy Department at the Bank of Thailand, adds: “ The insights on technical integration, operating models and regulatory considerations established a practical foundation for modernising wholesale settlement infrastructure.”

“The results provide a strong foundation for further collaboration as we explore how this approach could be developed towards real-world use,” says Tom Mutton, the Bank of England’s executive director of payments, innovation and fintech.
